source_text: ΕΙΣ ΤΟ "Ἀσπάσασθε Πρίσκιλλαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν," καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, λόγος αʹ. αʹ. Πολλοὺς ὑμῶν οἶμαι θαυμάζειν ἐπὶ τὴν περικοπὴν τῆς ἀποστολικῆς ἀναγνώσεως ταύτης, μᾶλλον δὲ πάρεργον ἡγεῖσθαι καὶ περιττὸν τοῦτο τῆς ἐπιστολῆς τὸ μέρος, διὰ τὸ προσρήσεις ἔχειν μόνον συνεχεῖς καὶ ἐπαλλήλους. Διὸ δὴ καὶ αὐτὸς ἑτέρωσε τήμερον ὡρμημένος, ἀποστὰς ἐκείνης τῆς ὑποθέσεως, εἰς ταύτην καθεῖναι παρασκευάζομαι, ἵνα μάθητε, ὅτι τῶν θείων Γραφῶν οὐδὲν περιττὸν, οὐδὲν πάρεργόν ἐστι, κἂν ἰῶτα ἓν, κἂν μία κεραία ᾖ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ψιλὴ πρόσρησις πολὺ πέλαγος ἡμῖν ἀνοίγει νοημάτων. Καὶ τί λέγω, ψιλὴ πρόσρησις; Πολλάκις καὶ ἑνὸς στοιχείου προσθήκη ὁλόκληρον νοημάτων εἰσήγαγε δύναμιν. Καὶ τοῦτο ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ Ἀβραὰμ προσηγορίας ἔστιν ἰδεῖν. Πῶς γὰρ οὐκ ἄτοπον παρὰ φίλου μὲν ἐπιστολὴν δεχόμενον, μὴ τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἐπιστολῆς ἀναγινώσκειν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν κάτω κειμένην πρόσρησιν, κἀκεῖθεν μάλιστα στοχάζεσθαι τὴν τοῦ γεγραφότος διάθεσιν, Παύλου δὲ γράφοντος, μᾶλλον δὲ οὐ τοῦ Παύλου, ἀλλὰ τῆς τοῦ Πνεύματος χάριτος τὴν ἐπιστολὴν ὑπαγορευούσης ὁλοκλήρῳ πόλει καὶ δήμῳ τοσούτῳ, καὶ δι' ἐκείνων τῇ οἰκουμένῃ πάσῃ, νομίζειν περιττόν τι εἶναι τῶν ἐγκειμένων, καὶ παρατρέχειν ἁπλῶς, καὶ μὴ ἐννοεῖν, ὅτι ταῦτα πάντα τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε; Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι, τοῦτο, ὃ πολλῆς ῥᾳθυμίας ἡμᾶς ἐνέπλησε, τὸ μὴ πάσας ἐπιέναι τὰς Γραφὰς, ἀλλ' ἃ νομίζομεν εἶναι σαφέστερα, ταῦτα ἐκλεγομένους, τῶν ἄλλων μηδένα ποιεῖσθαι λόγον. Τοῦτο καὶ τὰς αἱρέσεις εἰσήγαγε, τὸ μὴ βούλεσθαι ἅπαν ἐπιέναι τὸ σῶμα, τὸ νομίζειν εἶναί τι περιττὸν καὶ πάρεργον. Διὰ τοῦτο τὰ μὲν ἄλλα ἅπαντα ἡμῖν διεσπούδασται, οὐχὶ τὰ περιττὰ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἀνόνητα καὶ βλαβερά· τῶν Γραφῶν δὲ ἡ ἐμπειρία ἠμέληται καὶ παρῶπται· καὶ οἱ μὲν πρὸς τὴν θεω ρίαν τῆς τῶν ἵππων ἁμίλλης ἐπτοημένοι, καὶ ὀνόματα, καὶ ἀγέλην, καὶ γένος, καὶ πατρίδα, καὶ ἀνατροφὴν τῶν ἵππων ἔχουσιν εἰπεῖν μετὰ ἀκριβείας ἁπάσης, καὶ ἔτη ζωῆς, καὶ ἐνεργείας δρόμων, καὶ τίς τίνι συνταττόμενος τὴν νίκην ἁρπάσεται, καὶ ποῖος ἵππος ἐκ ποίας ἀφεθεὶς βαλβῖδος, καὶ τίνα ἔχων ἡνίοχον, περιέσται τοῦ δρόμου, καὶ τὸν ἀντίτεχνον παραδραμεῖται. Καὶ οἱ περὶ τὴν ὀρχήστραν δὲ ἐσχολακότες, οὐκ ἐλάττω τούτων, ἀλλὰ καὶ πλείω μανίαν περὶ τοὺς ἐν τοῖς θεάτροις ἀσχημονοῦντας ἐπιδείκνυνται, μίμους λέγω καὶ ὀρχηστρίας, καὶ γένος αὐτῶν, καὶ πατρίδα, καὶ ἀνατροφὴν, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα καταλέγοντες· ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐρωτώμενοι, ὁπόσαι, καὶ τίνες εἰσὶν αἱ Παύλου ἐπιστολαὶ, οὐδὲ τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἴσμεν εἰπεῖν. Εἰ δέ τινες καὶ εἶεν τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἐπιστάμενοι, ἀλλὰ τὰς πόλεις, αἳ τὰς ἐπιστολὰς ἐδέξαντο, ταύτας ἐρωτώμενοι διαποροῦσι πρὸς τὴν ἐρώτησιν. Καὶ ἄνθρωπος μὲν εὐνοῦχος καὶ βάρβαρος, μυρίαις φροντίσιν ὑπὸ μυρίων ἑλκόμενος πραγμάτων, οὕτω προσέκειτο βιβλίοις, ὡς μηδὲ κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ὁδοιπορίας ἡσυχάζειν, ἀλλ' ἐπ' ὀχήματος καθήμενος, ἐγκεῖσθαι μετὰ πολλῆς τῆς ἀκριβείας τῇ τῶν θείων Γραφῶν ἀναγνώσει· ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐδὲ τὸ πολλοστὸν μέρος τῆς ἀσχολίας ἔχοντες τῆς ἐκείνου, καὶ πρὸς τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν ἐπιστολῶν ξενιζόμεθα, καὶ ταῦτα καθ' ἑκάστην κυριακὴν ἐνταῦθα συλλεγόμενοι, καὶ θείας ἀπολαύοντες ἀκροάσεως.
thought_title: No part of Scripture is superfluous
orientation: Chrysostom opens his homily on Paul's greeting to Priscilla and Aquila by addressing his congregation about their neglect of Scripture's seemingly minor parts.
pass_a_gloss: On the "Greet Priscilla and Aquila," and the things following, homily one. 1. Many of you I think are amazed at the passage of this apostolic reading, or rather consider this part of the letter a side matter and superfluous, because it has only greetings continuous and successive. Therefore indeed I myself, having set out today in another direction, having departed from that subject, am preparing to descend into this one, in order that you may learn, that of the divine Scriptures nothing is superfluous, nothing is a side matter, not even one iota, not even one stroke, but even a bare greeting opens to us a great sea of thoughts. And why do I say, a bare greeting? Often even the addition of one letter introduced a whole power of thoughts. And this is possible to see in the case of the naming of Abraham. For how is it not absurd, when receiving a letter from a friend, not to read only the body of the letter, but also the greeting lying below, and from there especially to infer the disposition of the one who wrote, but when Paul writes, or rather not Paul, but the grace of the Spirit dictates the letter to a whole city and so great a people, and through those to the whole inhabited world, to consider any of the things contained in it superfluous, and to run past simply, and not to consider, that these things have turned everything upside down? For this is it, this, which has filled us with much carelessness, the not going through all the Scriptures, but choosing what we consider to be clearer, and making no account of the others. This also introduced the heresies, the not being willing to go through the whole body, the considering something to be superfluous and a side matter. Therefore all other things have been zealously pursued by us, not only the superfluous things, but also the useless and harmful things; but the experience of the Scriptures has been neglected and overlooked; and those who are excited at the spectacle of the horse race, can say with all accuracy the names, and herd, and breed, and homeland, and rearing of the horses, and years of life, and performances of races, and who, being matched with whom, will seize the victory, and which horse, released from which starting gate, and having which charioteer, will prevail in the race, and will outrun the rival. And those who have spent their leisure around the orchestra, display not less than these, but even more madness about those who act shamefully in the theaters, I mean mimes and dancing girls, recounting their family, and homeland, and rearing, and all the other things; but we, when asked, how many, and which are the letters of Paul, do not know how to say even the number. And if some do know the number, yet the cities, which received the letters, when asked about these they are at a loss at the question. And a man, a eunuch and a barbarian, being dragged by countless cares from countless affairs, so attended to books, that not even during the time of the journey did he rest, but sitting on a carriage, he applied himself with much accuracy to the reading of the divine Scriptures; but we, not having even the smallest part of the business of that man, are strangers even to the names of the letters, and this while gathering here every Lord's day, and enjoying divine hearing.

choices.why: Chrysostom contrasts it with the essential body of the letter; 'side matter' preserves the spatial metaphor of something beside the work.
The glossary mandates 'greeting' for πρόσρησις; the plural here refers to the repeated salutations in Romans 16.
Refers to the smallest mark of a letter, echoing Matthew 5:18; 'stroke' is the standard literal rendering.
Chrysostom's metaphor of a vast expanse of meaning; 'sea' keeps the image vivid and literal.
The Spirit is presented as the active author dictating the letter; 'dictates' preserves the agency and the metaphor of divine authorship.
Chrysostom diagnoses the congregation's neglect as moral laxity; 'carelessness' captures the ethical force.

bible_refs.note: the Ethiopian eunuch reading Scripture on his carriage

pass_b_english: I imagine many of you are puzzled by this passage from the apostolic reading, or rather consider this part of the letter a side matter and superfluous, because it contains only greetings, one after another in quick succession. That is why I myself, though I had set out today in another direction, have left that subject and am preparing to come down to this one, so that you may learn that in the divine Scriptures nothing is superfluous, nothing is a side matter—not one iota, not one stroke—but even a bare greeting opens a vast sea of meaning for us. And why do I say a bare greeting? Often the addition of a single letter has brought in the full force of whole thoughts. You can see this in the naming of Abraham. How absurd it would be, when you receive a letter from a friend, not to read only the body of the letter but also the greeting written at the bottom, and from that especially to infer the disposition of the writer—yet when Paul writes, or rather not Paul, but the grace of the Spirit dictating the letter to a whole city and so great a people, and through them to the entire world, to think that anything in it is superfluous, and to pass over it lightly, and not to consider that these attitudes have turned everything upside down? This is what has filled us with so much carelessness: that we do not go through all the Scriptures, but choose what we think is clearer and pay no attention to the rest. This is what has introduced heresies: the unwillingness to go through the whole body, the belief that something is superfluous and a side matter. That is why we have been diligent about everything else—not only the superfluous things, but even the useless and harmful ones—while skill in the Scriptures has been neglected and despised. Those who are excited about watching horse races can tell you with complete accuracy the names, the herd, the breed, the homeland, and the upbringing of the horses, and their years of life, and their performances in races, and which horse paired with which will seize the victory, and which horse released from which starting gate, and with which charioteer, will win the race and outrun its rival. And those who spend their time around the orchestra show no less madness than these—indeed even more—about those who disgrace themselves in the theaters, I mean the mimes and dancers, recounting their family, homeland, upbringing, and everything else. But when we are asked how many letters of Paul there are and which they are, we cannot even state the number. And if some do know the number, when asked about the cities that received the letters, they are at a loss to answer. A eunuch, a barbarian, pulled in ten thousand directions by ten thousand concerns, was so devoted to books that he did not rest even during his journey, but seated on his carriage he applied himself with great care to the reading of the divine Scriptures. Yet we, who do not have even the smallest fraction of his business, are strangers even to the names of the letters—and this though we gather here every Lord's day and enjoy listening to the divine Scriptures.

problems.quote: these things have turned the whole world upside down
problems.source_quote: ταῦτα πάντα τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε
problems.why: Greek means 'has made all these things up and down' i.e. thoroughly examined them; English idiom 'turned upside down' suggests revolution, not careful scrutiny.
problems.fix: has gone through all these things from top to bottom
problems.ruling: τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε means 'turned things upside down'; English 'whole world' adds κόσμος not in source, changing reference.

edits.old: these things have turned the whole world upside down
edits.new: has gone through all these things from top to bottom

fixed: Corrected mistranslation: 'ταῦτα πάντα τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε' means 'has made all these things up and down' i.e. thoroughly examined them, not 'turned upside down'.

problems.quote: and not to consider that has gone through all these things from top to bottom
problems.source_quote: καὶ μὴ ἐννοεῖν, ὅτι ταῦτα πάντα τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε
problems.why: Missing subject: 'he'/'Paul' who composed all these things
problems.fix: and not to consider that he has composed all these things from top to bottom

problems.quote: and not to consider that has gone through all these things from top to bottom?
problems.why: ἄνω κάτω ποιεῖν means 'turn upside down,' not 'go through from top to bottom.'
problems.fix: and not to consider that these things have turned all upside down?
problems.ruling: τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε means 'has turned upside down/confused,' not 'gone through from top to bottom'—meaning inverted.

edits.old: and not to consider that has gone through all these things from top to bottom?
edits.new: and not to consider that he has turned all these things upside down?

fixed: The English omitted the subject and mistranslated the idiom. The source 'ταῦτα πάντα τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε' means 'he has turned all these things upside down,' with Paul (or the Spirit) as the implied subject. The earlier edit was wrong; the idiom is 'turn upside down,' not 'go through from top to bottom.'

problems.quote: and not to consider that he has turned all these things upside down?
problems.source_quote: καὶ μὴ ἐννοεῖν, ὅτι ταῦτα πάντα τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε;
problems.why: Neuter plural ταῦτα ("these attitudes") is the subject of singular πεποίηκε, not the object of an implied "he"; these habits have turned everything upside down.
problems.fix: and not to realize that these very habits have turned everything upside down?
problems.ruling: ταῦτα πάντα (neuter plural) is subject of singular πεποίηκε with τὰ ἄνω κάτω; English wrongly supplies “he” and objects ταῦτα, inverting agency.

edits.old: and not to consider that he has turned all these things upside down?
edits.new: and not to consider that these attitudes have turned everything upside down?

fixed: agency: real error — ταῦτα πάντα is subject of singular πεποίηκε, so changed `he has turned all these things` to `these attitudes have turned everything`.

problems.why: Greek ἀκρόασις means listening to Scripture or preaching; 'the divine hearing' sounds like God's sense of hearing or a legal proceeding.
problems.fix: enjoy listening to the divine Scriptures
problems.ruling: ἀκροάσεως here is enjoying sacred listening or preaching; 'divine hearing' misleads as God's ear or a legal hearing.

edits.old: gather here every Lord's day and enjoy the divine hearing.
edits.new: gather here every Lord's day and enjoy listening to the divine Scriptures.

fixed: enjoy the divine hearing (θείας ἀπολαύοντες ἀκροάσεως): fixed — ἀκρόασις is our hearing of Scripture, changed to listening to the divine Scriptures

these things have turned the whole world upside down / ταῦτα πάντα τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε: no edit — current 'these attitudes have turned everything upside down' fairly renders ταῦτα as the dismissive acts just named
has gone through all these things from top to bottom / ταῦτα πάντα τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε: no edit — ἄνω κάτω is upside-down, not thorough review, current wording already correct
he has turned all these things upside down / ταῦτα πάντα τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε: no edit — current 'these attitudes have turned everything upside down' fits the heresy context, left alone

last_rejected.quote: that he has turned all these things upside down
last_rejected.source_quote: ὅτι ταῦτα πάντα τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε
last_rejected.why: Greek 'τα ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε' means 'has made the upper things lower' i.e. inverted priorities, not 'turned all these things upside down' which suggests Paul has inverted the contents of the letter. The sense is about Paul's humility/condescension in writing such greetings, or how he has lowered himself.
last_rejected.fix: that he has stooped to do all these things
last_rejected.ruling: τὰ ἄνω κάτω πεποίηκε idiomatically means 'turned upside down'; English correctly renders this.

last_rejected.quote: we have been diligent about everything else—not only the superfluous things, but even the useless and harmful ones
last_rejected.source_quote: τὰ μὲν ἄλλα ἅπαντα ἡμῖν διεσπούδασται, οὐχὶ τὰ περιττὰ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἀνόνητα καὶ βλαβερά
last_rejected.why: Greek says 'the other things have all been diligently pursued by us'—passive or middle voice, not 'we have been diligent'. More importantly, 'τὰ περιττὰ' here refers to worldly things that are superfluous, but the English 'superfluous things' echoes the earlier theological term and creates confusion. The contrast is: we pursue worldly things (which are superfluous, useless, harmful) but neglect Scripture.
last_rejected.fix: everything else has been pursued with zeal by us—not merely superfluous things, but useless and harmful ones as well
last_rejected.ruling: διεσπούδασται passive 'has been diligently pursued' = 'we have been diligent'; τὰ περιττὰ contextually clear.

last_rejected.quote: and with which charioteer, will win the race and outrun its rival
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ τίνα ἔχων ἡνίοχον, περιέσται τοῦ δρόμου, καὶ τὸν ἀντίτεχνον παραδραμεῖται
last_rejected.why: The Greek has 'περιέσται τοῦ δρόμου' (will survive/win the race) AND 'παραδραμεῖται' (will outrun). English merges these but 'win the race and outrun its rival' captures both. Actually this seems present. Re-checking: English has 'will win the race and outrun its rival'—yes, both verbs are there.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'win the race and outrun its rival' renders both περιέσται and παραδραμεῖται; nothing omitted.
